sentences.text: The genus name Elopteryx combines Ancient Greek words meaning 'marsh' and 'wing'.
Charles William Andrews named the type species Elopteryx nopcsai in 1913.
Andrews originally thought this creature was a pelecaniform seabird.
Kálmán Lambrecht established the family Elopterygidae in 1933.
In 1975, Harrison and Walker moved several specimens to the new family Bradycnemidae, describing them as gigantic two-meter-tall owls.
By 1978, Pierce Brodkorb proposed that these bones actually belonged to non-avian dinosaurs.
Dan Grigorescu and Eugen Kessler later suggested Elopteryx was a non-avian coelurosaurian dinosaur.
Since the 21st century, most research places Elopteryx within Maniraptora and Paraves.
The Paleobi Database currently lists its parent group as Alvarezsauridae.
A 2024 study by Stoicescu and colleagues argued Elopteryx is a paravian member of Avialae and that Balaur bondoc is likely a junior synonym.
This same 2024 research attributed a new femur specimen from Romania to Elopteryx, indicating it was secondarily flightless.
Fossils of Elopteryx come from Late Cretaceous rocks in Romania.
These remains date to the early-late Maastrichtian stage, roughly 70 to 66 million years ago, found in the Sânpetru Formation of the Hațeg Island.
The specific time range for the species spans from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.

In 2019, studies debated Elopteryx's classification, with some recovering it as a basal avialan confuciusornithiform and others suggesting it forms a clade with Gargantuavis and Balaur native to the Late Cretaceous European archipelago.
Stephen L. Brusatte and colleagues suggested in 2013 that Elopteryx and Balaur bondoc might be the same taxon, though they did not consider it the most likely scenario.
Researchers have claimed that the synonymy between Elopteryx and Balaur bondoc remains possible and requires further confirmation.
